newsitem.title: USA: TWA targets business travelers to revive traffic.
newsitem.headline: TWA targets business travelers to revive traffic.

text.p: Trans World Airlines Inc., in an effort to rebound from significant losses, plans to target business travelers this year as it adds more efficient aircraft.
TWA, whose independent auditors have raised concerns about its ability to continue as a going company, on Monday posted a first quarter net loss of $71.6 million.

"We are too much of a leisure travelers' airline and not enough of a business travelers' airline, and our fare mix reflects this," TWA Chairman Gerald Gitner said in a letter to shareholders that accompanied TWA's annual report and proxy statement.
The head of the nation's seventh-largest carrier outlined goals aimed at fixing problems that caused a net loss for 1996 and wiped out progress TWA felt it had made in the first half of the year.

"We tried to grow our system too fast (in 1996) ... and as a result we ended up with a schedule we could not fulfil and a level of reliability that cost us money and alienated customers," Gitner wrote.
Gitner acknowledged that 1996 was a rough year for TWA, which lost $285 million and suffered what Gitner described as a "personal loss" with the crash of TWA Flight 800 on July 17.

Gitner said 50 TWA workers, friends and family members were among the 230 people killed when the Boeing 747 jet crashed into the Atlantic Ocean minutes after taking off from New York en route to Paris.
The cause of the crash has yet to be determined. The National Transportation Safety Board plans to hold public hearings on the crash this summer.

Gitner promised an expanded marketing programme designed to offer business travelers what he described as "superior access to first-class upgrades, preferred customer service, special amenities and better frequent flyer benefits."
In the letter, TWA also explained to its shareholders the exact sequence of events that caused its financial problems as 1996 came to a close.

Gitner cited an ultimately unworkable large-scale growth plan that included the purchase of used 747 jets. He said late delivery of those planes led to schedule reliability problems, which caused higher overall maintenance and crew costs.
The higher expenses led to revenue loss from flight cancellations and passenger inconvenience, Gitner said.
Higher fuel prices and higher-than-expected contract maintenance costs added to the carrier's fiscal problems.

According to Gitner, TWA's near-term future will involve establishing a domestic mega-hub in St. Louis offering about 350 flights per day, and setting up an international and transcontinental hub at John F. Kennedy Airport in New York, where TWA currently offers flights to 11 foreign destinations.
Gitner said the carrier may add more international cities as its fleet is modernised with more fuel-efficient and less maintenance-intensive jets.
The carrier is already phasing out its 747s and L-1011 large-size jets in favour of Boeing 757 and 767 models, which are less costly to maintain, Gitner said.
As TWA accepts delivery on its first new aircraft orders since 1984, the average aircraft age will drop by 2.3 years over the course of 1997, Gitner said.
On Monday, the carrier reported a first-quarter net loss of $71.6 million, or $1.54 a share, vs. a loss of $37.1 million, or $1.46, in the same period last year.

A sharp reduction in TWA's cash reserves, which shrank to $136.5 million from $181.6 million at the end of December, caused some analysts to voice concern about TWA's ability to survive in the cyclical passenger airline business.
TWA is scheduled to hold its annual shareholder meeting May 29, where the election of five directors and the ratification of KPMG Peat Marwick as independent accountants are on the agenda.
TWA stock rose 18.75 cents Wednesday to $7.1875 in afternoon trading on the American Stock Exchaange.
